readerTitle: Two ways to pay for a second bakery, and what each one really costs
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 빵집 2호점, 소프트웨어 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용 · 적용 레슨: 부채 vs 지분, 희석
insight: 확장 자금을 지분으로 받으면 새 매장만이 아니라 이미 돈을 버는 기존 매장의 일부까지 내준다. 갚을 현금 흐름이 예측 가능하면 대출이, 불확실하면 지분이 맞다.
misconception: 대출은 이자가 붙으니 비싸고, 투자금은 갚을 필요가 없으니 공짜에 가깝다.

sources.text: 재무관리의 표준 개념 (부채와 지분의 차이, 지분 희석, 원리금 균등상환)

factChecks.note: 스트레스 테스트: 2호점 첫해 이익 $0 가정 시 기존 매장 $80,000 − 상환 $30,800 = $49,200 남음.
개인 보증 등 대출 조건은 나라와 은행마다 다르므로 일반적으로만 언급했습니다. 특정 국가의 법률·세무 조언은 하지 않습니다.

cards.title: Two ways to pay for a second bakery, and what each one really costs
body: Lena's bakery makes about $80,000 a year in profit. A shop across town is empty, and opening it would cost $120,000.
She has two offers on the table. One looks expensive. The other looks free. Neither is what it seems.

image.label: A bakery owner holding two envelopes in front of an empty shop
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 빵집 주인이 빈 상가 앞에서 봉투 두 개를 들고 있음. 한쪽 봉투에 "Bank loan", 다른 쪽에 "Investor" 라벨. 실제 은행이나 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which offer should Lena take?
body: **Offer 1:** a bank loan of $120,000 at 9% interest, repaid over five years.
**Offer 2:** a local investor gives $120,000 in exchange for 30% of the bakery. No repayments.
Her first shop has been steady for six years.

options.text: The loan. Her steady profits can cover the payments
options.feedback: This is **debt vs equity** at work. When cash is predictable, a loan costs a fixed amount and then ends, and Lena keeps all of her business.

options.text: The investor. No payments means no risk
options.feedback: It removes the monthly payments but adds a permanent partner. Equity has no due date, so it never stops costing.

options.text: Half and half, to spread the risk
options.feedback: A mix can make sense when cash is uncertain. Here it still gives away 15% of a proven shop to avoid payments she can already afford.

cards.title: Five years of each offer.
body: Assume the second shop adds $50,000 a year, so the bakery earns $130,000. The loan ends after five years. The investor's 30% never does, and it also covers any future sale.

cards.title: She'd be selling part of the first shop too.
body: **Dilution** means your share of the business shrinks when someone new buys in. The investor doesn't get 30% of the new shop. They get 30% of everything.
That includes the original bakery, which already earns $80,000 without any new money. Lena would be paying $24,000 a year from a shop that didn't need funding.

image.label: Two bakeries, both with a 30% slice shaded
image.brief: 빵집 두 곳을 원형 파이처럼 표현. 새 매장뿐 아니라 기존 매장에도 똑같이 30% 조각이 다른 색으로 칠해져 있음. 기존 매장 조각에 "Already profitable" 라벨.

cards.title: What if the new shop is slow?
body: New locations often take a while to find customers. Say the second shop earns nothing in its first year.
Can Lena still carry a $30,800 yearly payment?

options.text: Yes. The first shop's $80,000 still covers it, with about $49,000 left
options.feedback: **Debt vs equity** again: a loan fits when some steady cash can make the payments even in a bad year. Her pay gets tighter, but the bakery survives.

options.text: No. Any slow year means she can't pay
options.feedback: That would be true for a brand-new bakery with no track record. Lena's first shop is the safety net that makes debt workable.

options.text: Only if the new shop is profitable from month one
options.feedback: That's too strict. The question isn't whether the new shop pays for itself at once, but whether the whole business can cover the payment.

cards.title: The loan is cheaper only if the plan holds.
body: These numbers are forecasts. If the new shop loses money for two years, or a big oven breaks, fixed payments can squeeze the whole business.
Banks often ask small owners for a personal guarantee, which can put their own savings or home at stake. And a good investor can bring more than money: advice, contacts, a second pair of hands.
Run the slow-year numbers before signing anything.

cards.title: Now it's a young app.
body: A two-year-old budgeting app has growing users but still loses money each month. Revenue swings a lot. The founders want $300,000 to build a paid version.

options.text: A bank loan, so they keep 100% ownership
options.feedback: There's no steady cash to make payments. If the paid version is slow, a loan could sink the company. **Debt** needs predictable income.

options.text: An investor, accepting dilution to fund an uncertain bet
options.feedback: Equity fits when the payoff is uncertain and far away. **Dilution** hurts less here, because most of the company's value doesn't exist yet.

options.text: Founders' credit cards until the paid version launches
options.feedback: It avoids dilution, but it's high-interest debt with the same problem: no reliable cash to repay it.

cards.title: Match the money to how sure the cash is.
body: You used two ideas here. **Debt vs equity:** steady cash can carry a loan, uncertain cash needs a partner. **Dilution:** selling a share means selling part of what already works.
**Try it today:** if you needed money to grow, write down your worst-year profit. Could it cover a fixed yearly payment?
